title: Migraine Therapy: Match Acute and Preventive Treatment to Risk
bottomLine: Treat migraine as a recurrent neurologic disorder: confirm the phenotype and secondary-headache safety screen, choose acute therapy early in the attack, and add prevention when disability, frequency or acute-medication burden justifies it. A preventive drug is selected by comorbidity, pregnancy potential, adverse-effect profile and patient preference—not by memorizing one universal first choice.
recognize: Migraine typically causes recurrent attacks with nausea and/or sensory sensitivity and may include fully reversible aura.
Increasing use of acute medication can create medication-overuse headache and is itself a reason to reassess prevention.
differentiate: Thunderclap onset, new neurologic deficit, papilledema, fever/meningismus, pregnancy/postpartum severe headache or major pattern change requires secondary-cause evaluation before routine migraine treatment.
Cluster headache and tension-type headache have different phenotypes and treatment pathways.
assessment: Track attack frequency, duration, disability, aura, menstrual/hormonal pattern, pregnancy plans, vascular risk, acute-medication days per month and prior treatment response.
Assess sleep, caffeine, hydration, mood and other modifiable triggers without implying that lifestyle caused the disorder.
workup: Typical stable migraine with a normal neurologic examination generally does not require routine neuroimaging.
Use imaging or other testing only when red flags or an atypical pattern changes the pretest probability of secondary disease.
management: Use evidence-based acute therapy matched to severity and contraindications; migraine-specific therapy is appropriate when simple analgesics are ineffective or unsuitable.

Offer prevention when attacks are frequent/disabling, acute treatment is overused/contraindicated or patient preference supports it; select from guideline-supported oral, injectable or device options according to patient factors.
Reassess efficacy after an adequate therapeutic trial using attack frequency, disability and acute-medication use.
medicationSafety: Avoid vasoconstrictive acute agents when relevant vascular contraindications are present and use pregnancy-specific treatment review.
Preventive therapies have agent-specific mood, weight, BP, cognitive, teratogenic, renal and interaction considerations; do not copy one dose/titration plan across products.
counselling: Use a headache diary to connect treatment to frequency, disability and rescue-medication exposure.
Teach that prevention reduces attack burden over time and does not replace urgent evaluation of a new dangerous headache phenotype.
followUp: Review preventive response, tolerability and acute-medication burden after dose changes.
Refer for specialty care when diagnosis is uncertain, neurologic red flags emerge or disability persists despite adequate preventive trials.
examTrap: Escalating rescue medication repeatedly without recognizing medication-overuse headache or considering prevention.
oneLinePearl: Acute therapy stops today's migraine; prevention is for the pattern across months.
sourceBasis: Canadian Headache Society migraine guidance and 2024 prevention guideline
Choosing Wisely Canada headache imaging recommendations

title: Seizure Classification and Antiseizure Medication Selection
bottomLine: Classify the seizure/epilepsy syndrome before selecting long-term therapy. Drug choice depends on focal versus generalized onset, comorbidities, reproductive potential, interactions, organ function and adverse-effect risk; a medication that is effective for one seizure type may worsen another.
recognize: Focal seizures begin in one network and may occur with preserved or impaired awareness; generalized seizures engage bilateral networks from onset.
A first provoked seizure from hypoglycemia, sodium disturbance, withdrawal or another acute cause is not automatically epilepsy.
differentiate: Syncope, psychogenic nonepileptic events, movement disorders and sleep phenomena can mimic seizure.
Status epilepticus or recurrent seizures without recovery is an emergency and is separate from routine long-term medication selection.
assessment: Obtain witness description, prior subtle events, triggers, sleep, alcohol/substance changes, medications, pregnancy potential, mood, cognition, kidney/liver disease and prior adverse reactions.
Assess driving/occupation and safety risks from recurrent loss of awareness.
workup: Use EEG and appropriate MRI for unprovoked/focal presentations according to the seizure pathway; use cause-directed labs and imaging for provoked or atypical events.
Do not use a normal routine EEG as proof that a clinically convincing seizure did not occur.
management: Treat the seizure syndrome with an evidence-supported ASM matched to seizure type and patient factors.
After a first unprovoked seizure, estimate recurrence risk from syndrome, EEG, imaging and clinical context before committing to chronic therapy.
Refer complex, drug-resistant, pregnancy-related or diagnostically uncertain epilepsy to neurology.
medicationSafety: Valproate has major reproductive/teratogenic risk and requires strict risk assessment in people who could become pregnant.
Some sodium-channel ASMs can aggravate selected generalized epilepsies; enzyme-inducing ASMs can interact with contraception and many other drugs.
Abrupt discontinuation can precipitate seizures; tapering is drug- and context-specific.
redFlags: Serious ASM rash or organ toxicity
counselling: Discuss sleep, alcohol/substance triggers, adherence, pregnancy planning and driving/reporting rules applicable to the jurisdiction.
Teach that seizure control and medication toxicity are monitored together.
followUp: Track seizure frequency/type, adverse effects, adherence and disease-specific monitoring.
Reassess diagnosis if events continue unchanged despite adequate therapy or semiology is inconsistent.
examTrap: Choosing an antiseizure medication before identifying whether the patient has focal or generalized epilepsy.
oneLinePearl: Name the seizure network first; then choose the drug.
sourceBasis: Canadian pregnancy and antiseizure-medication safety principles

title: TIA: Transient Symptoms Can Signal Immediate Stroke Risk
bottomLine: TIA is a time-sensitive vascular syndrome, not a reassuring diagnosis because symptoms resolved. Recent focal motor or speech symptoms require rapid stroke-capable assessment, brain/vascular imaging and mechanism-directed secondary prevention; do not delay urgent evaluation while calculating a risk score.
recognize: Abrupt unilateral weakness/numbness, aphasia/dysarthria, monocular vision loss or other focal deficits can represent TIA when they resolve.
Motor and speech symptoms within the recent high-risk window carry substantial early recurrence risk.
differentiate: Migraine aura often evolves/spreads over minutes with positive phenomena; seizure may cause postictal deficit; hypoglycemia can mimic focal neurologic symptoms.
Syncope is global hypoperfusion and usually does not create a focal vascular syndrome.
assessment: Document exact onset, duration, symptom sequence, last-known-well, antithrombotics, AF history, vascular risk, prior stroke/TIA and residual findings.
Check glucose and perform focused neurologic/cardiovascular examination without delaying emergency transfer when the syndrome is high risk.
workup: Use urgent brain and vascular imaging plus ECG/rhythm assessment through the stroke/TIA pathway.
Risk scores may support disposition in some systems but must not replace imaging/mechanism assessment or override high-risk clinical features.
management: Activate urgent stroke/TIA care for recent high-risk symptoms.
Start antithrombotic and vascular risk treatment after hemorrhage/contraindications and mechanism are appropriately assessed through the pathway.
Identify carotid disease, AF and other treatable mechanisms quickly because time to intervention matters.
medicationSafety: Do not start anticoagulation simply because TIA is suspected without establishing AF/cardioembolic indication and bleeding context.
Dual antiplatelet therapy, when indicated, is time- and patient-specific and should not become indefinite treatment by default.
redFlags: Carotid-territory symptoms with severe stenosis concern
counselling: Teach that resolved symptoms can be the warning phase before a major stroke and still require emergency assessment.
Review FAST signs and recurrence instructions.
followUp: Ensure closed-loop stroke-clinic/neurology follow-up, vascular imaging, rhythm monitoring and secondary-prevention ownership.
examTrap: Scheduling routine outpatient neurology because symptoms resolved before arrival.
oneLinePearl: TIA is a disappearing symptom with a very real near-term stroke risk.
sourceBasis: Canadian Stroke Best Practices TIA/minor stroke recommendations
Canadian Stroke Best Practices secondary prevention guidance

title: Parkinson Disease: Diagnose the Syndrome, Treat Function, Watch for Atypical Features
bottomLine: Parkinson disease is a clinical syndrome centred on bradykinesia plus characteristic motor features. Treatment is based on functional impact and patient priorities; early falls, gaze palsy, severe early autonomic failure or poor levodopa response should trigger reconsideration of atypical parkinsonism.
recognize: Bradykinesia with rest tremor and/or rigidity, often asymmetric initially, supports parkinsonism.
Nonmotor symptoms include constipation, anosmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, depression, cognitive change and autonomic symptoms.
differentiate: Essential tremor is primarily action/postural; drug-induced parkinsonism may be more symmetric and follows dopamine-blocking exposure.
Atypical parkinsonism is suggested by early falls, vertical gaze palsy, early severe autonomic dysfunction, prominent cerebellar signs or poor dopaminergic response.
assessment: Assess gait/freezing/falls, dexterity, speech/swallowing, cognition, mood, orthostasis, sleep, bowel/bladder function and medications that block dopamine.
Ask which symptoms impair the patient's actual daily function before escalating therapy.
workup: Diagnosis is primarily clinical; routine imaging does not confirm typical PD but can assess alternative diagnoses when atypical features are present.
management: Use dopaminergic therapy individualized to symptom burden, age and adverse-effect risk; integrate exercise, physiotherapy, OT and speech/swallow support.
Address constipation, orthostasis, mood, sleep and cognition as active parts of the disease.
Refer atypical, rapidly progressive or treatment-complicated disease to neurology/movement-disorders care.
medicationSafety: Do not abruptly interrupt levodopa/dopaminergic therapy in hospitalized patients unless clinically unavoidable; severe rigidity/hyperthermia syndromes can occur.
Dopamine agonists can cause impulse-control disorders, hallucinations and sleep attacks; dopamine-blocking antiemetics/antipsychotics can worsen parkinsonism.
redFlags: Acute inability to take dopaminergic medication
counselling: Teach medication timing, falls prevention, constipation/orthostasis strategies and driving safety.
Ask caregivers about impulse-control behaviours and cognition because patients may not volunteer them.
followUp: Track motor fluctuations, dyskinesia, gait/falls and nonmotor burden.
Reassess diagnosis when progression or treatment response is atypical.
examTrap: Treating tremor alone as Parkinson disease without demonstrating bradykinesia.
oneLinePearl: Parkinson disease starts with bradykinesia; treatment targets function, not the tremor score alone.

title: Essential Tremor: Action Tremor With a Functional Treatment Goal
bottomLine: Essential tremor is a predominantly bilateral action/postural tremor syndrome diagnosed clinically after medication, metabolic and other neurologic causes are considered. Treat only when tremor meaningfully affects function or quality of life, and choose therapy around comorbidities and adverse-effect risk.
recognize: Hands/arms are most commonly affected during posture or action; head or voice tremor may occur.
Family history and alcohol responsiveness can occur but are not required for diagnosis.
differentiate: Parkinson tremor is usually rest-predominant with bradykinesia/rigidity; enhanced physiologic tremor can follow anxiety, caffeine, hyperthyroidism or medications.
Cerebellar tremor is accompanied by ataxia/dysmetria and changes the workup.
assessment: Characterize activation condition, distribution, symmetry, onset/progression and effect on eating, writing, work and social function.
Review stimulants, bronchodilators, valproate/lithium and thyroid symptoms; perform a focused neurologic examination for parkinsonism/cerebellar signs.
workup: No routine imaging is needed for a classic stable essential-tremor phenotype; order thyroid/metabolic or imaging studies only when history/examination suggests an alternative cause.
management: Mild non-disabling tremor may need education only.
Use guideline-supported first-line pharmacotherapy such as propranolol or primidone when functional impairment warrants treatment, individualized to patient comorbidity.
Refer refractory severe tremor for specialist options including advanced pharmacologic or procedural therapies.
medicationSafety: Propranolol may be unsuitable with significant asthma, bradycardia or selected cardiac conditions; primidone can cause sedation/ataxia, especially during initiation.
Avoid escalating medication when the main issue is a reversible stimulant/drug exposure.
counselling: Set treatment goals around tasks the patient wants to regain rather than complete tremor suppression.
Discuss caffeine/stimulant modification when relevant without blaming the patient for the disorder.
followUp: Track functional improvement and medication adverse effects.
Reconsider the diagnosis if bradykinesia, ataxia or other neurologic features emerge.
examTrap: Calling a bilateral action tremor Parkinson disease because the patient is older.
oneLinePearl: Essential tremor is an action tremor; treat the disability, not the visible movement alone.

title: Multiple Sclerosis: Relapse, Mimic, and Disease-Modifying Therapy
bottomLine: MS diagnosis requires objective evidence of CNS demyelination disseminated in time and space after important mimics are excluded. New symptoms are not automatically relapse: infection, fever and heat can reproduce old deficits. Disease-modifying therapy is selected with neurology according to disease activity, safety profile, pregnancy plans and patient preference.
recognize: Optic neuritis, partial myelitis, brainstem/cerebellar syndromes and sensory/motor deficits are common demyelinating presentations.
Pseudo-relapse reproduces prior symptoms during fever/infection/metabolic stress without new inflammatory activity.
differentiate: Stroke, cord compression, B12 deficiency, neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorders and other inflammatory/infectious diseases can mimic MS.
Progressive disability without distinct relapses may represent a progressive phenotype rather than recurrent acute attacks.
assessment: Define whether symptoms are new, objective and sustained; ask about infection, bladder symptoms, heat, pregnancy/postpartum status and current DMT.
Assess vision, strength, sensation, gait, cerebellar/brainstem function and sphincter symptoms.
workup: MRI brain/spinal cord and CSF are used to support diagnosis and disease activity under neurology; serologic testing is targeted to mimics.
Do not diagnose relapse from subjective fatigue alone without assessing infection and objective neurologic change.
management: Treat functionally significant relapse with specialist-guided corticosteroid therapy when appropriate after important infection is addressed.
Use DMT to reduce new inflammatory activity; selection/escalation depends on efficacy, infection risk, monitoring burden, pregnancy and patient preference.
Rehabilitation, symptom management, vaccination and preventive care are part of long-term management.
medicationSafety: DMTs have agent-specific CBC/liver/infection/vaccine/PML and pregnancy requirements; there is no universal monitoring schedule.
Do not abruptly stop or switch a high-efficacy DMT around pregnancy without specialist planning because rebound disease can occur with selected agents.
counselling: Discuss pregnancy early, vaccination timing, smoking cessation, fatigue and rehabilitation.
Explain the difference between relapse and pseudo-relapse so infection-driven symptom worsening is not automatically treated with steroids.
followUp: Coordinate longitudinal neurologic monitoring of disease activity, disability and DMT safety.
Reassess new symptoms promptly when the pattern does not fit prior MS activity.
examTrap: Giving high-dose steroids for transient worsening during a UTI without assessing pseudo-relapse first.
oneLinePearl: New MS symptoms need two questions: is this new inflammation, and is there a trigger reproducing old deficits?

title: Peripheral Neuropathy: Pattern, Tempo, and Cause
bottomLine: Peripheral neuropathy workup starts by defining distribution, tempo and motor/autonomic involvement. A slowly progressive distal symmetric sensory neuropathy has a different differential from focal mononeuropathy, multifocal disease or rapidly ascending weakness; testing should follow the pattern rather than becoming an indiscriminate lab panel.
recognize: Length-dependent sensory loss, paresthesias, reduced ankle reflexes and gait instability are common in distal symmetric polyneuropathy.
Diabetes, alcohol, B12 deficiency, CKD, medications/chemotherapy and monoclonal gammopathy are common causes.
differentiate: Radiculopathy follows a nerve-root pattern; myelopathy causes upper-motor-neuron signs and may include a sensory level/bowel-bladder dysfunction.
Rapidly progressive symmetric weakness with areflexia raises Guillain-Barré syndrome and changes disposition urgently.
assessment: Map sensory loss, strength, reflexes, gait, autonomic symptoms and foot integrity; ask about diabetes, alcohol, medications/toxins, nutrition, family history and systemic symptoms.
Look for asymmetry, marked motor weakness or upper-motor-neuron signs that make routine distal neuropathy less likely.
workup: Use targeted glucose/A1C, B12, CBC, renal/thyroid and monoclonal-protein testing when clinically appropriate.
EMG/NCS is useful for atypical, motor, asymmetric, rapidly progressive or diagnostically uncertain neuropathy.
management: Treat the cause when possible, protect insensate feet and address falls risk.
Use neuropathic-pain therapy only when symptoms warrant it and titrate around sedation, renal function and comorbidity.
Refer atypical, progressive motor or immune-mediated patterns to neurology.
medicationSafety: Gabapentinoids and sedating antidepressants increase falls/respiratory-sedation risk, especially with opioids or frailty.
Avoid escalating symptom medication while missing a reversible cause such as B12 deficiency, medication toxicity or glucose dysregulation.
counselling: Teach foot inspection and injury prevention when protective sensation is impaired.
Set expectations that neuropathic-pain drugs reduce symptoms rather than restore nerve function.
followUp: Track progression, gait/falls and cause-specific response.
Escalate the workup if the pattern becomes asymmetric, motor-predominant or rapidly progressive.
examTrap: Ordering a huge neuropathy panel before determining whether the process is distal symmetric, focal, root-level or central.
oneLinePearl: Draw the neuropathy map before ordering the tests.

title: Dementia: Diagnose the Syndrome, Find Reversible Contributors, Plan Longitudinal Care
bottomLine: Dementia is acquired cognitive decline that interferes with independence. Establish chronicity and affected domains, distinguish it from delirium/depression, identify reversible contributors, determine likely etiology and build a safety/caregiver plan. Disease-modifying Alzheimer therapies are specialist-selected and biomarker-/stage-specific, not routine treatment for any memory complaint.
recognize: Memory, executive, language, visuospatial and behavioural changes may occur; functional decline differentiates dementia from isolated subjective complaint.
Collateral history is often essential because insight may be limited.
differentiate: Delirium is acute/fluctuating with impaired attention; depression can mimic cognitive impairment but does not explain every progressive syndrome.
Lewy body, vascular, frontotemporal and Alzheimer phenotypes have different clinical clues and medication sensitivities.
assessment: Assess onset/progression, ADLs/IADLs, medications/anticholinergic burden, sleep, mood, hearing/vision, substance use, falls, driving, finances, medication management and caregiver stress.
Assess capacity for the decision at hand rather than labeling all patients with dementia globally incapable.
workup: Use a validated cognitive tool plus neurologic/functional assessment; obtain targeted CBC, electrolytes/renal, TSH, B12 and imaging when appropriate to the syndrome.
Specialty biomarker testing is used when it changes etiologic diagnosis or disease-modifying treatment decisions.
management: Treat reversible contributors, optimize vascular/sensory health and use cholinesterase inhibitor/memantine therapy when indicated for the dementia subtype/stage.
Address driving, medication/financial safety, home supports, advance care planning and caregiver needs early.
Refer atypical, young-onset, rapidly progressive or disease-modifying-therapy candidates to specialty care.
medicationSafety: Cholinesterase inhibitors can cause bradycardia/syncope, GI effects and weight loss; anticholinergic drugs can worsen cognition.
Disease-modifying monoclonal therapies require specialist confirmation, MRI/bleeding-risk monitoring and eligibility assessment; do not present them as routine memory drugs.
counselling: Use person-centred language and include caregivers with consent while preserving autonomy where capacity remains.
Start future planning while the person can participate meaningfully.
followUp: Track cognition, function, safety, caregiver burden and treatment adverse effects.
Reassess the diagnosis when the course becomes atypical or new neurologic features appear.
examTrap: Diagnosing dementia during an acute fluctuating hospitalization without addressing delirium first.
oneLinePearl: Dementia is cognitive decline plus lost independence; delirium is acute brain failure.
sourceBasis: Alzheimer Society of Canada clinical education resources

title: Delirium: Acute Brain Failure Until a Cause Is Found
bottomLine: Acute fluctuating inattention and cognitive change is delirium until proven otherwise. Find and treat the precipitating medical cause, restore orientation/mobility/sleep/sensory input and avoid routine sedative/restraint strategies; medication is reserved for narrow dangerous-agitation situations and does not cure delirium.
recognize: Delirium can be hyperactive, hypoactive or mixed; hypoactive delirium is easily missed.
Common precipitants include infection, hypoxia, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, medication toxicity, withdrawal and environmental disruption.
differentiate: Dementia is chronic/progressive and can coexist with delirium; depression does not usually produce fluctuating inattention.
A positive urine culture without a compatible urinary/infectious syndrome does not prove UTI caused the delirium.
assessment: Establish baseline cognition from collateral history; assess attention, fluctuation, oxygenation, glucose, pain, retention/constipation, medications, withdrawal, hydration and neurologic findings.
Look for sepsis, stroke, hypoxia or other acute instability first.
workup: Use targeted CBC/chemistry/ECG/imaging/urine studies based on the suspected cause; avoid routine neuroimaging or urine testing without clinical indication.
management: Correct causes; orient/reassure, mobilize, use hearing/vision aids, support sleep/wake cycle and involve familiar supports.
Avoid restraints/lines/catheters when possible and reserve antipsychotic medication for severe dangerous distress/agitation after reversible causes and non-drug measures are addressed.
Treat alcohol/benzodiazepine withdrawal with the appropriate withdrawal pathway rather than the usual delirium approach.
medicationSafety: Benzodiazepines worsen most non-withdrawal delirium and increase falls/sedation.
Anticholinergics, opioids, sedatives and polypharmacy are common medication contributors; review necessity and dose.
redFlags: Dangerous agitation with inability to maintain safety
counselling: Explain to families that delirium is an acute medical syndrome and cognition may recover gradually after the trigger is corrected.
Avoid telling families that a sudden decline is simply dementia progression.
followUp: Reassess cognition after recovery because delirium can reveal underlying cognitive disease.
Document the precipitant and medication changes clearly across transitions of care.
examTrap: Treating asymptomatic bacteriuria solely because an older patient is confused.
oneLinePearl: Delirium is a symptom of acute illness; treat the trigger, not the confusion alone.

title: Meningitis and Encephalitis: Treat the Syndrome Before Every Test Is Perfect
bottomLine: Fever with meningismus, altered mental status, seizure or rapidly evolving neurologic illness is a time-critical CNS infection syndrome. Obtain cultures and CSF when safe, but never create a harmful antibiotic/acyclovir delay while waiting for nonessential imaging or a perfect lumbar puncture sequence.
recognize: Bacterial meningitis can present with fever, headache, neck stiffness, photophobia, altered consciousness or rash, but classic findings may be incomplete.
Encephalitis is suggested by altered behaviour/consciousness, focal deficits or seizures with infectious features.
differentiate: Subarachnoid hemorrhage, severe sepsis/toxic-metabolic encephalopathy, migraine and intracranial mass can mimic parts of the syndrome.
HSV encephalitis may occur without prominent meningismus and requires antiviral coverage when plausible.
assessment: Assess ABCs, GCS, seizure, focal deficits, rash, immune status, recent infection/travel, antibiotic exposure and contraindications to immediate LP.
Use isolation precautions promptly when meningococcal disease is possible.
workup: Obtain blood cultures and CSF studies when safe; head imaging before LP is reserved for features that raise concern for mass effect/herniation risk rather than performed routinely for every case.
Do not delay empiric therapy for imaging/LP when bacterial meningitis or encephalitis is strongly suspected.
management: Start age/risk-appropriate empiric IV antimicrobials promptly and add acyclovir when encephalitis is plausible.
Use dexamethasone and public-health/contact-management measures when indicated by the bacterial/meningococcal pathway.
Manage seizures, shock, raised-ICP concerns and respiratory failure in acute care.
medicationSafety: Renal function affects acyclovir and selected antimicrobial dosing; hydration/renal monitoring matters with IV acyclovir.
Antimicrobial allergy history must not create an unsafe delay—use an appropriate alternative regimen with urgent expert input.
counselling: Explain why treatment may begin before every diagnostic result is available.
Coordinate public-health contact management when meningococcal disease is suspected/confirmed.
followUp: Ensure pending cultures/PCR and public-health actions are closed-loop.
Arrange hearing/neurocognitive follow-up after bacterial meningitis when indicated.
examTrap: Waiting for CT and lumbar puncture before giving antibiotics to a deteriorating patient with a strong bacterial meningitis syndrome.
oneLinePearl: In CNS infection, diagnostics should inform treatment—not postpone it.
sourceBasis: Canadian infectious-disease and emergency-neurology practice principles
Public Health Agency of Canada meningococcal resources
